title: Seven trillion spores
teaches: How fungi spread by spores, how gills launch them, and why most land close while a few cross oceans
summary: **A spore does a seed's job for a fungus.** One or a few cells with a tough wall, a few thousandths of a millimetre across, that can start a new mycelium.
**Fungi make spores in enormous numbers.** Buller estimated seven trillion from one giant puffball; almost all of them die.
**Small spores fall very slowly.** Fall speed goes with the square of size, so a tiny spore drifts far on the faintest breeze.
**Most spores still land near home.** The few that are carried up above the trees can travel for days.
**A mushroom shoots each spore off with a drop of water.** Buller's drop merges with a film on the spore, and the jolt throws it a tenth of a millimetre.
**Gills must hang very nearly vertical.** Tilt a cap and the spores hit the gills; mushrooms bend their stems to stay upright.
**Other fungi use rain, animals and insects.** Puffballs are pumped by raindrops, truffles eaten, stinkhorns visited by flies.

blocks.text: The giant puffball, *Calvatia gigantea*, grows in late summer on meadows and field edges as a smooth white ball, often the size of a football and sometimes far bigger. As it ripens, its inside turns from firm white flesh to an olive-brown powder, and the skin cracks. Kick an old one and it lets out a cloud of brown smoke. The smoke is spores.

Early in the twentieth century A. H. Reginald Buller, a mycologist at the University of Manitoba in Winnipeg, estimated how many. He measured the spores, measured the puffball, and worked out how many would pack into it: about seven trillion, a seven followed by twelve zeros.[^buller] Each spore can in principle start a new fungus. If every one of them grew into a puffball that made seven trillion more, within two generations the puffballs, at a kilogram or so each, would weigh many times as much as the Earth.

There is no shortage of meadows full of puffballs because nearly all those spores die. They land somewhere too dry, too shaded, already taken, or simply on the wrong food. A mushroom does not aim its spores. It makes so many that a few land well. This lesson is about how a spore gets from where it was made to where it might grow.

A **spore** is a single cell, or a small group of cells, with a thick wall, often darkened with pigment that shields it from ultraviolet light. It carries a copy of the fungus's genes and a little stored food, enough to put out a first hypha if it lands somewhere damp with something to eat. Many spores can wait, dry and inactive, for months or years.

Spores are small. Most are between about 3 and 20 thousandths of a millimetre (micrometres, µm) across, too small to see one at a time with the naked eye. A drift of them is visible as colour: the white, cream, pink, brown or black dust that falls from a mushroom cap left gills-down overnight on paper, a spore print. Some fungi make spores after mating, which the next lesson follows; most also make spores without it, as copies of themselves. The blue-green powder on a mouldy orange is chains of such copies.

Something very small falls very slowly through air, because the air's drag matters more and more as size shrinks. For a speck the size of a spore, the speed it settles at goes with the square of its width.[^stokes] A spore 10 µm across falls about 3 millimetres a second, about as fast as a snail crawls. Half that width and it falls four times slower. A dust-fine spore takes minutes to fall the height of a mushroom.

blocks.caption: A spore dropping from a cap 8 cm above the ground in a steady breeze. Change the spore's size and the wind. A model of still air with a steady wind, so it leaves out gusts and updrafts, which only lengthen the trip.
blocks.task: Try the smallest spores, then the largest

blocks.text: Even so, most spores land close to home. Near the ground, under trees and among grass, the air is nearly still, and spore counts fall off steeply within a few metres of a mushroom. What matters is the small share that escape: a spore lifted above the canopy by an eddy or a warm afternoon can stay aloft for days and travel hundreds or thousands of kilometres. Spores have been caught in air samples kilometres up, and fungi turn up quickly on new volcanic islands and in sterilised soil left open to the air.

A mushroom does not simply let its spores fall. Each spore sits on a short prong on a cell on the surface of a gill, and when it is ripe it is thrown off. Buller watched this through a microscope aimed sideways at a gill. Just before a spore leaves, a tiny drop of water appears at its base and swells; then the spore and drop vanish, too fast for his eye to follow. The drop is still called **Buller's drop**.

How the drop throws the spore was not worked out until high-speed cameras could film it, in the 1990s and 2000s. The spore's surface collects water from the humid air in two places: the drop at its base and a thin film on its side. When the drop grows big enough to touch the film, the two merge in a few millionths of a second. The water of the drop is pulled sideways into the film, so its weight shifts suddenly along the spore, away from the prong. The jolt snaps the spore off its prong with an acceleration of thousands of times gravity's, and it flies about a tenth of a millimetre.

blocks.caption: Buller's drop, the catapult that throws a spore off a mushroom gill, in three steps over a few millionths of a second. Greatly magnified: the spore is about a hundredth of a millimetre long.

blocks.text: A tenth of a millimetre is a very short flight, and that is the point. It carries the spore off the gill into the gap between gills, where it stops and falls straight down, out under the cap, into the air below. A spore shot further would hit the gill opposite.

Gills multiply a mushroom's spore-making surface many times over: a cap with a few hundred gills has the area of a sheet of paper or more packed under it, and it can shed billions of spores in a few days. The price is precision. The gaps between gills are under a millimetre wide and the gills several millimetres deep, so a falling spore has a narrow, deep slot to fall down.

blocks.caption: Two gills seen edge on, magnified, with spores shot from each face and then falling. Tilt the cap. A model; the gills are drawn much shallower than real ones, to fit.
blocks.task: Guess, then tilt until most spores are caught

blocks.text: So mushrooms keep their gills vertical. A stem grows upward against gravity and holds the cap level, so its gills hang straight down. Knock a mushroom over and within hours its stem bends near the top to bring the cap level again. Mushrooms with tubes under the cap instead of gills, such as the spongy-capped boletes, face the same problem, and their tubes hang just as straight.

Not every fungus throws its spores. A puffball is a bag with a hole in the top. When a raindrop hits its thin skin, the skin dents and puffs out a cloud of spores, and a single shower can empty a good part of it. Bird's-nest fungi hold their spores in tiny egg-like packets in a cup a centimetre across; a raindrop landing in the cup splashes them out up to a metre or so.

Others pay animals. Stinkhorns cover their spores in a slime that smells of rotting meat and is eaten by flies, which leave with spores on their feet and in their guts. Truffles fruit underground, where no wind can reach, and ripen with a smell that draws animals to dig them up and eat them; branch N follows one such partnership in Northwest forests. And some of the smallest fungi shoot. The dung fungus *Pilobolus* fires its whole spore packet more than two metres, aimed at the light, clear of the patch of grass around the dung that cattle will not eat, onto grass they will.[^pilobolus]

blocks.caption: Five questions on spores
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why does a fungus make billions or trillions of spores?
choices: Almost all of them land where they cannot grow
Each spore can grow only a few hyphae
Spores need to fuse in large groups to grow
items.why: A fungus cannot aim its spores. Nearly every one dies, so the few that land on suitable food somewhere are enough only because so many are made.

items.ask: Spore A is half the width of spore B. Roughly how does its fall speed in still air compare?
choices: Both fall at the same speed
items.why: For something as small as a spore, settling speed goes with the square of width. Half the width means a quarter of the speed, and four times as long in the air.

items.ask: What throws a spore off a mushroom gill?
choices: A drop of water merging with a film on the spore, which jolts it free
Air rushing between the gills when the cap dries
The gill snapping straight after bending
items.why: Buller's drop grows at the spore's base until it touches a film of water on the spore's side. When they merge, the shift of weight throws the spore about a tenth of a millimetre.

items.ask: Why must a mushroom's gills hang very nearly straight down?
choices: Spores fall straight down a narrow, deep gap, and a slight tilt puts a gill in their way
A tilted cap loses water too fast
Spores can only be launched upward
items.why: The gaps are under a millimetre wide and several millimetres deep. Tilt a few degrees and many falling spores land on a gill instead of dropping out below.

items.ask: How does a puffball release its spores?
choices: Raindrops dent its thin skin, puffing spores out of a hole
It shoots each spore off a prong, like a mushroom
Animals dig it up and eat it underground
items.why: A ripe puffball is a bag of loose spores with an opening. Each raindrop or knock squeezes it, and a puff of spores comes out.

buller.title: Buller
buller.text: Arthur Henry Reginald Buller, born in Birmingham in 1874, spent most of his career at the new University of Manitoba. His seven-volume *Researches on Fungi* appeared from 1909 to 1950.

stokes.title: Stokes's law
stokes.text: For a sphere small enough that air flows smoothly round it, the drag is proportional to its width times its speed, while its weight goes with the cube of its width. A falling spore soon reaches the speed at which drag balances weight, and setting the two equal gives a settling speed proportional to the width squared, a result George Stokes derived in 1851.

pilobolus.title: The hat thrower
pilobolus.text: *Pilobolus* grows on herbivore dung. Its stalk swells with water under a dark spore packet and bursts, firing the packet as far as two or three metres toward the brightest light. The packet sticks to grass, a grazing animal eats it, the spores pass through its gut, and the fungus grows on the new dung.
